parts.title: Front Page Trouble
parts.text: Tessa, the editor of the Maple Street Middle School newspaper, stared at the empty front page. The **deadline** for Friday's edition was only two days away. Malik, the paper's sports **correspondent**, burst in with exciting news: a **rumor** was racing through the halls that the principal planned to cancel the spring dance.

parts.title: Chasing the Facts
parts.text: Grace, who wrote the weekly **editorial**, was already drafting a **persuasive** essay urging the principal to reconsider. Tessa stopped her. "We don't print **gossip**," she said. "We need facts first." Malik wanted a **sensational** headline in giant red letters: DANCE DESTROYED! Tessa shook her head. Instead, they tracked down an **eyewitness**, the office assistant, who had actually heard the principal's phone call.

parts.title: Setting It Straight
parts.text: The assistant explained that the dance was not canceled at all. A leaky roof meant it would simply move to the gym. Tessa also learned that a new reporter had planned to **fabricate** a quote from the principal to make the story more exciting. She gave him a firm but fair **rebuke**: "Readers trust us only when every word is true." Malik had already posted a teaser online, so he had to **retract** it with a public correction. The real story ran with his **byline** at the top.

parts.title: Truth First
parts.text: On Friday, the paper sold out in minutes. Tessa pinned the corrected story to the wall as a reminder that a newsroom's most important job is protecting the truth. Grace joked that the spring dance now had the best publicity in school history, even if it had been shuffled into the gym.

definitions.meaning1: A newspaper article that gives the opinion of the editors or writers. Example: Grace wrote an editorial urging the school board to keep the library open.
definitions.meaning2: Having to do with editing or editors. Example: The editorial team checked every sentence for errors.
definitions.studentChallenge: The paper's ___ argued that the school should add a bike rack.

definitions.meaning1: The time or date by which something must be finished. Example: The project has a strict deadline of Friday at noon.
definitions.studentChallenge: She worked through the night to meet the ___ for her science report.

definitions.meaning1: A story passed from person to person that may not be true. Example: A rumor spread that a famous author would visit our school.
definitions.studentChallenge: Don't believe every ___ you hear in the cafeteria; many aren't true.

definitions.meaning1: To take back something you said or wrote, admitting it was wrong. Example: The paper had to retract its false story and print a correction.
definitions.meaning2: To pull back or draw in. Example: A cat can retract its claws when it walks quietly.
definitions.studentChallenge: The website had to ___ the article after learning the facts were wrong.

definitions.meaning1: To make up something false in order to fool people. Example: It is wrong to fabricate a quote just to make a story more exciting.
definitions.meaning2: To build or manufacture something. Example: The factory will fabricate steel beams for the new bridge.
definitions.studentChallenge: A dishonest writer might ___ an interview that never happened.

definitions.meaning1: Casual talk about other people's private lives, often unkind or untrue. Example: Mia refused to listen to any gossip about her friend.
definitions.meaning2: A person who loves to talk about other people's private lives. Example: The town gossip knew everyone's business.
definitions.studentChallenge: Spreading ___ about classmates can hurt their feelings.

definitions.meaning1: A line at the top of an article that names the writer. Example: Tessa was thrilled to see her name in the byline above her first front-page story.
definitions.studentChallenge: The reporter's name appeared in the ___ above the headline.

definitions.meaning1: A reporter who sends news from a particular place or about a particular subject. Example: The paper's foreign correspondent sent reports from three countries.
definitions.meaning2: A person who writes letters regularly. Example: My grandmother is a faithful correspondent who writes every month.
definitions.studentChallenge: The television ___ reported live from the storm zone.

definitions.meaning1: To scold someone sharply for doing something wrong. Example: The coach had to rebuke the team for arriving late.
definitions.meaning2: A sharp scolding. Example: His rude joke earned him a stern rebuke from the principal.
definitions.studentChallenge: The teacher had to ___ the class for ignoring the fire drill.

definitions.meaning1: Able to convince people to believe or do something. Example: Her persuasive speech convinced the whole class to start recycling.
definitions.studentChallenge: The lawyer made such a ___ argument that the jury agreed at once.

definitions.meaning1: Designed to shock or excite people, often by exaggerating. Example: The tabloid used a sensational headline to shock readers.
definitions.meaning2: Extremely good; amazing. Example: The singer gave a sensational performance.
definitions.studentChallenge: The newspaper's ___ headline made a small event sound like a disaster.

definitions.meaning1: A person who sees an event happen and can describe it. Example: Police asked the eyewitness to describe exactly what she saw.
definitions.studentChallenge: The ___ told the reporter exactly how the accident happened.
